name: HAL LCH Prachand (Light Combat Helicopter)

header.one_liner: India's indigenous light combat helicopter; 15 delivered (IAF + Army), 156 on order end-FY26; optimised for high-altitude CAS; Shakti engine (Safran licence); first IAF LCH unit No. 143 'Gunbirds' operational.

at_a_glance.Engine: 2 × HAL/Safran (Turbomeca) Shakti turboshaft — same as Dhruv
at_a_glance.Service_ceiling: 6,500 m (21,300 ft) — optimised for high-altitude CAS

what_it_is.prose: The HAL LCH Prachand (Light Combat Helicopter) is India's indigenous dedicated combat helicopter, developed by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) based on the Dhruv ALH platform but with significant modifications for the combat role including stealth features (low radar cross-section), crashworthy armour, and a 20mm M621 chin-mounted cannon (Nexter, France). The LCH is optimised for high-altitude Close Air Support (CAS) operations — a critical requirement highlighted by the 2020 Galwan Valley clash with China in Eastern Ladakh. The LCH has a Maximum Take-Off Weight of 5,800 kg, payload of 1,500 kg external, and a service ceiling of 6,500 m (21,300 ft) — higher than the Dhruv. Armament includes the 20mm cannon, 70mm rockets, the Helina (Dhruvastra) Anti-Tank Guided Missile (DRDO-designed), Mistral-2 Within-Visual-Range Air-to-Air Missile (MBDA France), and reported counter-drone capability. The LCH is powered by two HAL/Safran Shakti turboshaft engines (same as the Dhruv). The indigenous content is approximately 65%. The first Limited Series Production (LSP) LCH was delivered to the IAF in 2022, with 15 delivered cumulatively to the IAF and Indian Army as of end-FY26. The first IAF LCH unit is No. 143 Squadron 'Gunbirds'. HAL had 156 LCH Prachand on order at the end of FY26 (part of the ₹2,54,538 crore order book). The LCH was deployed operationally in Eastern Ladakh during the 2020 standoff, demonstrating its high-altitude CAS capability. The LCH is named 'Prachand' (Sanskrit for 'fierce' or 'intense').

faq.question: What is the difference between the HAL Dhruv and the HAL LCH Prachand?
faq.answer: The HAL Dhruv is a multirole transport helicopter (Advanced Light Helicopter). The HAL LCH Prachand is a dedicated combat helicopter derived from the Dhruv platform but with significant modifications including stealth features (low radar cross-section), crashworthy armour, a 20mm M621 chin-mounted cannon, and dedicated weapon stations. The LCH is optimised for high-altitude Close Air Support (CAS) — a requirement highlighted by the 2020 Galwan Valley clash. Both share the same Shakti engine.

faq.question: Why was the LCH Prachand developed?
faq.answer: The LCH Prachand was developed to meet the Indian armed forces' requirement for a dedicated combat helicopter optimised for high-altitude operations — particularly in Eastern Ladakh and along the Line of Actual Control with China. The 2020 Galwan Valley clash underscored this requirement. The LCH has a service ceiling of 6,500 m (21,300 ft), higher than the Dhruv, allowing it to operate in mountainous terrain where conventional attack helicopters cannot. The Mi-35 (IAF's previous attack helicopter) was retired in 2022, making the LCH the IAF's primary attack helicopter.

faq.question: How many LCH Prachand does India operate?
faq.answer: As of end-FY26, 15 LCH Prachand had been delivered to the IAF and Indian Army, with 156 on order (part of HAL's ₹2,54,538 crore order book). The first IAF LCH unit is No. 143 Squadron 'Gunbirds'. HAL is ramping up production capacity at Bengaluru to meet the large order book. The first Limited Series Production (LSP) LCH was delivered in 2022.
